message: Operation 'searchAddresses' has semantic quality issues: vague_summary, missing_output_details. Summary 'Suggest addresses as someone types' is too generic and doesn't convey the specific prefix-matching behavior or G-NAF-only scope. Description is comprehensive but dense; simplified version clarifies the key distinction from typeahead, unit handling, and emphasizes the importance of storing the id for AI agents to understand data persistence patterns.

data.current_description:
G-NAF only. Unlike `/v1/typeahead`, which also returns suburbs and places, every result here is a resolved address, so nothing has to be filtered out.

Matching is a prefix of the street line, so type it as it is written: number first, then the street. A unit in front is understood and resolves to the unit's own record, not the building's: `3/90 Bay Road` returns the pid of unit 3, and `90 Bay Road` returns the pid of the parcel. `unit 3`, `u3`, `apt 3` and `3 90` are read the same way. A trailing postcode narrows.

Each result carries its `id`. Store that, not the text: the text is however your user typed it that day, the id is the address. An Australian result carries the same value under `address_detail_pid`, which is G-NAF's own column name.
data.summary_suggestion: Autocomplete G-NAF addresses with prefix matching
data.description_suggestion: Search G-NAF addresses by prefix matching on the street line. Returns resolved address records only (unlike `/v1/typeahead` which includes suburbs and places). Supports unit notation (`3/90 Bay Road`, `unit 3`, `u3`, `apt 3`, `3 90`) and postcode filtering. Each result includes `id` (or `address_detail_pid`) which should be stored for future reference rather than the typed text, as the id is the canonical address identifier.
data.reasoning: Summary 'Suggest addresses as someone types' is too generic and doesn't convey the specific prefix-matching behavior or G-NAF-only scope. Description is comprehensive but dense; simplified version clarifies the key distinction from typeahead, unit handling, and emphasizes the importance of storing the id for AI agents to understand data persistence patterns.

Summary 'Find addresses close to one that is misspelled' assumes misspelling but doesn't clarify it's a fallback mechanism. data.current_summary: Find addresses close to one that is misspelled
data.current_description:
For when `/v1/addresses/resolve` found nothing. An address typed by a person is wrong often enough that "no match" is not a useful final answer: `1 gorge rd sydenhum` is one address, and saying which is the point.

The suburb is corrected first, then street lines within it are scored by similarity. Include the suburb if you have it — it is what keeps this fast, and it is what makes the correction good.

**This is the expensive endpoint.** Every other address call is a prefix seek; this is a similarity scan, and it costs three units accordingly. Call it once on an address that failed to resolve, never on a keystroke — use `/v1/addresses` for that.
data.summary_suggestion: Find similar addresses when resolution fails
data.description_suggestion: Fuzzy-match addresses when `/v1/addresses/resolve` returns no match. Corrects suburb first, then scores street lines by similarity within that suburb. Provide the suburb if available to improve accuracy and performance. **Warning: This is an expensive operation (costs 3 units per call) as it performs similarity scanning rather than prefix matching. Use only after resolution fails, never on keystroke events—use `/v1/addresses` for real-time autocomplete instead.**

data.current_summary: Suggest addresses, suburbs and places as someone types
data.current_description:
Two characters minimum: below that the endpoint returns an empty list rather than matching most of the table.

Debounce by at least 150ms in the client. Each request is a unit, and firing on every keystroke spends them for no better answer.

A result whose `kind` is `address` is a resolved G-NAF record, not a string: it carries `gnaf_pid`, coordinates, and `components` holding the address split into G-NAF's own fields. Store the pid against your own record and the two systems agree they mean the same door, whatever either of you does to the formatting afterwards.

Address matching is a prefix of the street line, so type it the way it is written: the number first, then the street. A unit in front is understood and resolves to the unit's own record, not the building's: `3/90 Bay Road` returns the pid of unit 3, and `90 Bay Road` returns the pid of the parcel. `unit 3`, `u3`, `apt 3` and `3 90` are read the same way. A suburb name or a postcode alone matches suburbs, not addresses.
data.summary_suggestion: Unified autocomplete for addresses, suburbs, and places
data.description_suggestion: Real-time search across G-NAF addresses, suburbs, and places. **Minimum 2 characters required** (returns empty list below threshold). Results include three kinds: `address` (resolved G-NAF records with `gnaf_pid`, coordinates, and `components`), `suburb`, and `place`. Store the `gnaf_pid` for addresses to maintain system agreement on identity. Address matching uses prefix matching on street line (number first, then street); units (`3/90 Bay Road`, `unit 3`, `u3`, `apt 3`, `3 90`) resolve to their own records. **Client-side debouncing of 150ms+ recommended** to conserve units (each request costs 1 unit).

Description is comprehensive but scattered; reorganized to highlight minimum character requirement upfront, clarify the three result kinds with their properties, and consolidate performance/cost guidance. message: Operation 'searchAddresses' has semantic quality issues: vague_summary, missing_output_details. Summary 'Suggest addresses as someone types' is too generic and doesn't convey the specific prefix-matching behavior or G-NAF-only scope. Description is comprehensive but dense; simplified version clarifies the key distinction from typeahead, unit handling, and emphasizes the importance of storing the id for AI agents to understand data persistence patterns.

data.current_description:
G-NAF only. Unlike `/v1/typeahead`, which also returns suburbs and places, every result here is a resolved address, so nothing has to be filtered out.

Matching is a prefix of the street line, so type it as it is written: number first, then the street. A unit in front is understood and resolves to the unit's own record, not the building's: `3/90 Bay Road` returns the pid of unit 3, and `90 Bay Road` returns the pid of the parcel. `unit 3`, `u3`, `apt 3` and `3 90` are read the same way. A trailing postcode narrows.

Each result carries its `id`. Store that, not the text: the text is however your user typed it that day, the id is the address. An Australian result carries the same value under `address_detail_pid`, which is G-NAF's own column name.
data.summary_suggestion: Autocomplete G-NAF addresses with prefix matching
data.description_suggestion: Search G-NAF addresses by prefix matching on the street line. Returns resolved address records only (unlike `/v1/typeahead` which includes suburbs and places). Supports unit notation (`3/90 Bay Road`, `unit 3`, `u3`, `apt 3`, `3 90`) and postcode filtering. Each result includes `id` (or `address_detail_pid`) which should be stored for future reference rather than the typed text, as the id is the canonical address identifier.
data.reasoning: Summary 'Suggest addresses as someone types' is too generic and doesn't convey the specific prefix-matching behavior or G-NAF-only scope. Description is comprehensive but dense; simplified version clarifies the key distinction from typeahead, unit handling, and emphasizes the importance of storing the id for AI agents to understand data persistence patterns.

data.current_summary: Find addresses close to one that is misspelled
data.current_description:
For when `/v1/addresses/resolve` found nothing. An address typed by a person is wrong often enough that "no match" is not a useful final answer: `1 gorge rd sydenhum` is one address, and saying which is the point.

The suburb is corrected first, then street lines within it are scored by similarity. Include the suburb if you have it — it is what keeps this fast, and it is what makes the correction good.

**This is the expensive endpoint.** Every other address call is a prefix seek; this is a similarity scan, and it costs three units accordingly. Call it once on an address that failed to resolve, never on a keystroke — use `/v1/addresses` for that.
data.summary_suggestion: Find similar addresses when resolution fails
data.description_suggestion: Fuzzy-match addresses when `/v1/addresses/resolve` returns no match. Corrects suburb first, then scores street lines by similarity within that suburb. Provide the suburb if available to improve accuracy and performance. **Warning: This is an expensive operation (costs 3 units per call) as it performs similarity scanning rather than prefix matching. Use only after resolution fails, never on keystroke events—use `/v1/addresses` for real-time autocomplete instead.**

data.current_summary: Suggest addresses, suburbs and places as someone types
data.current_description:
Two characters minimum: below that the endpoint returns an empty list rather than matching most of the table.

Debounce by at least 150ms in the client. Each request is a unit, and firing on every keystroke spends them for no better answer.

A result whose `kind` is `address` is a resolved G-NAF record, not a string: it carries `gnaf_pid`, coordinates, and `components` holding the address split into G-NAF's own fields. Store the pid against your own record and the two systems agree they mean the same door, whatever either of you does to the formatting afterwards.

Address matching is a prefix of the street line, so type it the way it is written: the number first, then the street. A unit in front is understood and resolves to the unit's own record, not the building's: `3/90 Bay Road` returns the pid of unit 3, and `90 Bay Road` returns the pid of the parcel. `unit 3`, `u3`, `apt 3` and `3 90` are read the same way. A suburb name or a postcode alone matches suburbs, not addresses.
data.description_suggestion: Real-time autocomplete for addresses, suburbs, and places with prefix matching. **Minimum 2 characters required**; shorter queries return empty results. Results include three kinds: `address` (resolved G-NAF records with `gnaf_pid`, coordinates, and `components`), `suburb`, and `place`. Store the `gnaf_pid` for addresses to maintain system interoperability. Address matching uses prefix matching on the street line (number first, then street); unit notation (`3/90 Bay Road`, `unit 3`, `u3`, `apt 3`, `3 90`) resolves to the unit's own record. Suburb names or postcodes alone match suburbs, not addresses. **Client-side debouncing of at least 150ms is recommended** to reduce unit consumption (each request costs 1 unit).

Reorganized to clarify: minimum character requirement upfront, result types and their structure, address matching rules, and cost implications.
